title: Deiphobus. Bivium. Tartarus
titleEn: Deiphobus and the Gates of Tartarus — Aeneid VI.509–607
part: Deiphobus and the Gates of Tartarus (VI.509–607)
about: Deiphobus answers Aeneas: his friend has left nothing undone, and has paid every due to his shade. It was his own fate and the deadly crime of the Spartan woman, Helen, that sank him in these sufferings. On Troy's last night, when the wooden horse had leapt the walls, Helen, pretending to lead the Trojan women in a Bacchic dance, stood among them with a great torch and signalled to the Greeks from the citadel. Deiphobus, worn out, lay asleep in their chamber; his excellent wife cleared the house of weapons, slipped his sword from under his head, and opened the doors to Menelaus, hoping no doubt to buy her husband's favour and blot out the memory of her old wrongs. Menelaus and Ulysses, the prompter of crimes, burst in. Deiphobus prays the gods to pay the Greeks back in kind, and asks in turn what brings Aeneas alive to these sunless places. The day above is already past its middle, and the Sibyl cuts the talk short: night is coming on, and they are wasting the hours in tears. Here the road divides: the right-hand way runs beneath the walls of Dis and leads to Elysium, the left takes the wicked to their punishment in Tartarus. Deiphobus bids his friend go on to a better destiny than his own, and turns away. Looking back, Aeneas sees on the left a broad fortress with a triple wall, ringed by Phlegethon, the river of fire, with a gate of adamant that no god could break and an iron tower where Tisiphone keeps watch night and day; from inside come groans, the crack of whips and the clank of dragged chains. The Sibyl explains that no pure soul may set foot there, but that Hecate once led her through it all. Cretan Rhadamanthus rules this place: he punishes and hears the cases of those who hid their crimes in life, and forces them to confess; Tisiphone and her sisters lash and terrify them. Within the gates is a fifty-headed Hydra, and Tartarus itself goes down twice as deep as Olympus stands high. There lie the Titans, struck down by the thunderbolt; the giant sons of Aloeus who tried to pull down heaven; Salmoneus, who drove his chariot through Elis with a torch, mimicking Jupiter's thunder, and was hurled down by the true bolt; Tityos, whose vast body covers nine acres while a vulture feeds for ever on his liver; and those over whom a black rock hangs, ever about to fall, while a royal feast is spread before them and the eldest of the Furies, torch in hand, stops them from touching it.

sentences.t:
Ad quae Priamides: “Nihil O tibi amice relictum;
omnia Deiphobo solvisti et funeris umbris.
sentences.l:
To which Priam's son: “Nothing, O friend, by you has been left;
all to Deiphobus you have paid, and to the shades of the corpse.
sentences.i: Priam's son replied: “My friend, you have neglected nothing; every due to Deiphobus and to the shade of his body you have paid in full.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Deiphobus's answer to Aeneas's question at the end of the last part (500–508). 'Ad quae Priamides' leaves out the verb of speaking, as so often: 'in reply to which (said) the son of Priam'; 'quae' is a connecting relative, and 'Priamides' a Greek patronymic. The opening mark begins his speech, which runs to 534. 'Nihil… relictum (est)' is 'nothing has been left (undone)', and 'tibi' is a dative of the agent with the perfect passive. 'O' with a capital is Greenough's way with the interjection (compare 'O virgo', 560); it goes with the vocative 'amice', which he prints without commas. 'Solvisti' is 'you have paid', as one pays a debt: the empty tomb and the threefold call (505–506) were the dues owed to the dead. Deiphobus names himself in the third person, 'to Deiphobus'. 'Funeris' here is 'of the corpse', a sense of 'funus' given by Lewis & Short, and 'umbris' is a poetic plural for his one shade.

sentences.t:
Sed me fata mea et scelus exitiale Lacaenae
his mersere malis; illa haec monumenta reliquit.
sentences.l:
But me my fates and the deadly crime of the Laconian woman
in these have sunk evils; she these memorials left.
sentences.i: No, it was my own destiny and the deadly wickedness of the woman from Sparta that plunged me into this misery; these are the keepsakes she left me.
sentences.n: 'Sed' sets his own fate against Aeneas's care for him. 'Lacaenae' is 'the Laconian woman', Helen, wife of Menelaus king of Sparta in Laconia; Deiphobus will not speak her name. She had married Deiphobus after Paris was killed. 'Mersere' is 'merserunt', the '-ere' perfect (you'll see this constantly), 'plunged', 'drowned'. 'His… malis' is 'in these miseries', the mutilations Aeneas sees. 'Illa' is emphatic, 'she', and 'monumenta' is bitter: 'reminders', 'keepsakes', as if the wounds were tokens to remember her by. The Latin Library has the old spelling 'monimenta', the same word.

sentences.t:
Namque ut supremam falsa inter gaudia noctem
egerimus, nosti; et nimium meminisse necesse est.
sentences.l:
For how the last amid false joys night
we spent, you know; and too much to remember it is needful.
sentences.i: For you know how we passed that final night in a gladness that deceived us; and you have reason enough, and more, to remember it.
sentences.n: 'Ut… egerimus' is an indirect question, 'how we spent', with the perfect subjunctive, depending on 'nosti'. 'Nosti' is the shortened form of 'novisti', 'you know'. 'Inter' is placed after 'falsa' and before 'gaudia', framed by its phrase: 'amid false joys', the Trojans' celebration of the Greeks' supposed departure, told by Aeneas in Book II (2.248–249). 'Supremam… noctem' spans the line, 'the last night' of Troy. 'Nimium meminisse necesse est' is 'it is all too necessary to remember': Aeneas lived through it himself.

sentences.t:
Cum fatalis equus saltu super ardua venit
Pergama, et armatum peditem gravis attulit alvo,
illa, chorum simulans, evantes orgia circum
ducebat Phrygias;
sentences.l:
When the fateful horse with a leap over the steep came
Pergama, and armed infantry heavy brought in its belly,
she, a dance pretending, crying the Bacchic cry in the rites round
was leading the Phrygian women;
sentences.i: When the horse of destiny had come leaping over the steep walls of Pergama, its belly heavy with armed men, she made a show of leading a dance, and took the Phrygian women round in procession, raising the Bacchic cry in the rites;
sentences.n: 'Fatalis equus' is the wooden horse, 'fateful' because it brought Troy's doom. 'Saltu super… venit' is 'came with a leap over': a bold picture, since in Book II the Trojans breach their own walls to drag it in (2.234). 'Ardua… Pergama' runs over the line-end; Pergama, a neuter plural, is the citadel of Troy, and so Troy itself. 'Armatum peditem' is a collective singular, 'armed foot-soldiers'; 'gravis' is predicative, 'heavy (with them)', and 'alvo' is 'in its belly'. 'Illa' is Helen again. 'Chorum simulans' is 'pretending a dance'. 'Evantes' is from 'euhans', 'crying euhoe', the cry of Bacchus's worshippers (the Latin Library spells it 'euhantis'); 'orgia', 'the Bacchic rites', is its object, 'celebrating the rites with the cry of euhoe', and 'circum' is an adverb, 'round about'. 'Phrygias' is 'the Phrygian (women)', the Trojan women, held to the end of its clause. Behind the scene may lie Odyssey 4.271–289, where Helen walks round the horse with Deiphobus beside her, calling to the hidden Greeks in the voices of their wives.

sentences.t:
flammam media ipsa tenebat
ingentem, et summa Danaos ex arce vocabat.
sentences.l:
a flame in the middle she herself was holding,
huge, and from the highest citadel the Danaans she was calling.
sentences.i: she herself stood in their midst holding up a great torch, and from the top of the citadel she called the Greeks in.
sentences.n: 'Media ipsa' is 'she herself in the middle', among the dancing women. 'Flammam… ingentem' runs over the line-end, 'a huge flame', a torch held up as a signal. 'Summa… ex arce' is 'from the top of the citadel', and 'Danaos', 'the Danaans', is one of the old names for the Greeks. In Book II the signal fire is raised by the Greek king's flagship (2.256–257); Deiphobus gives Helen's part in it, perhaps to blacken her further, a different story of the same night.

sentences.t:
Tum me, confectum curis somnoque gravatum,
infelix habuit thalamus, pressitque iacentem
dulcis et alta quies placidaeque simillima morti.
sentences.l:
Then me, worn out with cares and with sleep weighed down,
the unhappy held chamber, and pressed me lying
a sweet and deep rest, and to peaceful most like death.
sentences.i: Then I, worn out with my cares and heavy with sleep, lay in that ill-starred bridal room, and as I lay a sweet deep rest weighed on me, the very likeness of quiet death.
sentences.n: 'Confectum curis' is 'exhausted by anxieties'; 'somno… gravatum' is 'weighed down with sleep'. 'Infelix… thalamus' is 'the ill-fated bedchamber', the marriage-chamber he shared with Helen: 'thalamus' is the word for the bridal room. 'Pressit… iacentem' is 'pressed (me) as I lay'. The subject is the whole next line, 'dulcis et alta quies'. 'Morti' is the dative with 'simillima', 'most like death', and 'placidae' agrees with 'morti'. The phrase is modelled on Homer's sleep of Odysseus on the Phaeacian ship, 'most like to death' (Odyssey 13.80), and here it is sweet sleep with death close behind it.

sentences.t:
Egregia interea coniunx arma omnia tectis
amovet, et fidum capiti subduxerat ensem;
sentences.l:
The excellent meanwhile wife all the weapons from the house
removes, and the trusty from my head had stolen sword;
sentences.i: Meanwhile my admirable wife cleared every weapon from the house; she had already slipped my trusty sword from under my head;
sentences.n: 'Egregia… coniunx', 'my outstanding wife', is bitterly ironic. 'Tectis' is an ablative of separation, 'from the house' ('tecta', 'roofs', is the house). 'Amovet' is a historic present; the Latin Library's 'emovet', 'moves out', comes to the same thing. The sudden pluperfect 'subduxerat' is 'had (already) stolen away': before she began clearing the house, the sword was gone. 'Capiti' is a dative of separation, 'from his head': warriors slept with their swords beside their pillows.

sentences.t:
intra tecta vocat Menelaum, et limina pandit,
scilicet id magnum sperans fore munus amanti,
et famam exstingui veterum sic posse malorum.
sentences.l:
within the house she calls Menelaus, and the threshold opens,
no doubt this a great hoping would be gift to her lover,
and that the fame be blotted out of old thus could her wrongs.
sentences.i: she called Menelaus into the house and threw open the doors, hoping, no doubt, that this would be a handsome gift to her lover, and that the story of her old misdeeds could be wiped out in this way.
sentences.n: 'Vocat' and 'pandit' are historic presents. 'Limina pandit' is 'opens wide the doors', 'limina' standing for the doorway. 'Scilicet', 'of course', 'no doubt', is sarcastic. 'Sperans' governs two accusative and infinitive constructions: 'id… fore munus magnum', 'that this would be a great gift', and 'famam exstingui… posse', 'that the report could be extinguished'. 'Amanti' is 'to her lover', and the sting is that the lover is Menelaus, her lawful husband, whom she had deserted for Paris. 'Veterum… malorum' is 'of her old wrongs', her flight to Troy, framed round 'sic posse'.

sentences.t: Quid moror?
sentences.l: Why do I delay?
sentences.i: Why should I draw this out?
sentences.n: 'Quid moror?' is 'why do I delay?', a formula for cutting a story short. 'Quid' is 'why', an adverbial accusative.

sentences.t:
Inrumpunt thalamo; comes additur una
hortator scelerum Aeolides.
sentences.l:
They burst into the chamber; a companion is added together,
the prompter of crimes, the son of Aeolus.
sentences.i: They burst into the bedroom, and with Menelaus came another, the instigator of crimes, the son of Aeolus.
sentences.n: 'Inrumpunt' is Greenough's spelling of 'irrumpunt'. 'Thalamo' is a dative of direction, 'into the chamber', common in verse. 'Comes additur una' is 'a companion is added along with (him)'; 'una' is the adverb, 'together'. The Latin Library's 'additus' changes nothing. 'Hortator scelerum' is 'urger of crimes', a word for one who eggs others on. 'Aeolides', 'son of Aeolus', is Ulysses, and the name is an insult: a hostile story made him the son not of Laertes but of Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, the most cunning of men. Odysseus and Menelaus go together to the house of Deiphobus in Odyssey 8.517–520.

sentences.t:
Di, talia Grais
instaurate, pio si poenas ore reposco!
sentences.l:
Gods, such things on the Greeks
renew, if with dutiful penalties mouth I demand back!
sentences.i: You gods, pay the Greeks back in the same coin, if the punishment I ask is asked with righteous lips!
sentences.n: 'Di' is the vocative plural of 'deus'. 'Instaurate' is 'renew', 'repeat': let the Greeks suffer the same. 'Grais' is the dative, 'for the Greeks'. 'Pio… ore' frames the clause, 'with righteous mouth', and 'si' is placed late: the prayer is qualified with 'if what I demand is just', a formula of prayer. 'Reposco' is 'demand back', 'demand as due'.

sentences.t:
Sed te qui vivum casus, age, fare vicissim,
attulerint.
sentences.l:
But you, what alive chances, come, speak in turn,
have brought.
sentences.i: But come, it is your turn: tell me what has brought you here alive.
sentences.n: The order is 'sed, age, fare vicissim qui casus te vivum attulerint'. 'Qui… casus' is 'what chances', interrupted by 'age, fare vicissim', 'come, speak in turn', and 'attulerint' is held over to the next line: an indirect question with the perfect subjunctive. 'Fare' is the imperative of the deponent 'for', 'speak'. 'Vivum' is the point: Aeneas is a living man among the dead.

sentences.t:
Pelagine venis erroribus actus,
an monitu divom?
sentences.l:
By the sea's do you come wanderings driven,
or by the warning of the gods?
sentences.i: Do you come driven here by wanderings over the sea, or by a warning from the gods?
sentences.n: 'Pelagine' is 'pelagi' with the question-particle '-ne' attached: 'of the sea?', going with 'erroribus', 'by wanderings (over) the sea'. 'An' introduces the second half of a double question, 'or'. 'Monitu' is 'by the warning'. 'Divom' is the old genitive plural of 'divus', 'of the gods' (the Latin Library has 'divum', the same form).

sentences.t:
An quae te Fortuna fatigat,
ut tristes sine sole domos, loca turbida, adires?”
sentences.l:
Or what you fortune harries,
that sad without sun homes, places confused, you should approach?”
sentences.i: Or what turn of fortune drives you on, to bring you to these gloomy homes where no sun shines, this troubled place?”
sentences.n: 'An quae… Fortuna' is 'or what fortune', and 'fatigat' is 'wears out', 'hounds'. 'Ut… adires' is a clause of result, 'that you should come to'; the imperfect after the present 'fatigat' looks back on the coming as already done. 'Tristes… domos' frames 'sine sole': 'gloomy homes without sun'. 'Loca turbida' is in apposition, 'places of confusion', murky and troubled. 'Tristes' is the '-es' accusative plural, 'tristis' in the Latin Library. The closing mark ends Deiphobus's speech.

sentences.t:
Hac vice sermonum roseïs Aurora quadrigis
iam medium aetherio cursu traiecerat axem;
sentences.l:
In this exchange of talk, with rosy Aurora her four-horse car
now the middle in her heavenly course had crossed of the sky;
sentences.i: While they talked in turn, Aurora with her rosy team had already passed in her heavenly course the middle of the sky;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Hac vice sermonum' is 'in this interchange of words'; 'vice' is 'turn', 'exchange'. 'Roseïs' carries a diaeresis in Greenough's print: the two dots tell you that 'e' and 'i' are separate vowels, ro-se-is, three syllables, not a diphthong. 'Quadrigis' is 'with her four-horse chariot', an ablative of means. 'Medium… axem' frames the line, 'the middle of the sky': 'axis' is the pole of heaven, then heaven itself. In the world above it is past midday. Aurora, goddess of the dawn, stands loosely for the day's light; the visit seems to have a time allotted to it, and half of it is spent.

sentences.t:
et fors omne datum traherent per talia tempus;
sed comes admonuit, breviterque adfata Sibylla est:
sentences.l:
and perhaps all the granted they would have drawn out in such talk time;
but his companion warned him, and briefly spoke the Sibyl:
sentences.i: and they might well have spent all the time allowed them in such talk, but his companion warned him, and the Sibyl said briefly:
sentences.n: 'Fors', the noun 'chance', is used here as an adverb, 'perhaps', like 'forsitan'. 'Traherent' is the imperfect subjunctive, potential in the past, 'they would have drawn out'. 'Omne datum… tempus' is framed round 'traherent per talia', 'all the time given': the visit is granted, not open-ended. 'Comes' is the Sibyl, Aeneas's companion on the journey. 'Adfata… est' is the perfect of the deponent 'adfor', 'address', with 'est' held to the end; 'adfata' is Greenough's spelling of 'affata'. The colon opens her words.

sentences.t: “Nox ruit, Aenea; nos flendo ducimus horas.
sentences.l: “Night rushes on, Aeneas; we in weeping spend the hours.
sentences.i: “Night is sweeping down, Aeneas, and we are passing the hours in tears.
sentences.n: The opening mark begins the Sibyl's speech, which runs to 543. 'Ruit' is 'rushes', of night coming on fast. 'Aenea' is the Greek vocative. 'Flendo' is the ablative of the gerund, 'by weeping', and 'ducimus' is 'we draw out', 'we spend'.

sentences.t: Hic locus est, partes ubi se via findit in ambas:
sentences.l: This is the place, into parts where the way splits itself both:
sentences.i: This is the place where the road divides and goes two ways:
sentences.n: 'Ubi' comes late in its clause. 'Se… findit' is 'splits itself', and 'partes… in ambas' is 'into both directions'. 'Partes' is the '-es' accusative plural ('partis' in the Latin Library). The fork in the road between the blessed and the damned recalls the myth at the end of Plato's Gorgias (524a), where the dead are judged at a meeting of roads, one leading to the Isles of the Blest and one to Tartarus; Virgil probably has it in mind.

sentences.t:
dextera quae Ditis magni sub moenia tendit,
hac iter Elysium nobis; at laeva malorum
exercet poenas, et ad impia Tartara mittit.”
sentences.l:
the right one, which of Dis the great beneath the walls stretches,
this way is the path to Elysium for us; but the left of the wicked
works the punishments, and to unholy Tartarus sends.”
sentences.i: the right-hand way, which runs below the walls of mighty Dis, is our road to Elysium; but the left carries out the punishment of the wicked, and sends them down to impious Tartarus.”
sentences.n: 'Dextera (via) quae… tendit' is 'the right (way), which stretches', taken up by 'hac', 'by this (way)'. 'Ditis magni… moenia' is 'the walls of great Dis', the palace of the king of the dead, where Aeneas must leave the golden bough (630–636). 'Elysium' is an accusative of goal, 'to Elysium', the home of the blessed, which they reach a little later (637–639). 'Iter… nobis' is 'the way for us', a dative with the verb left out. 'Laeva', 'the left (way)', is the side of ill omen. 'Exercet poenas' is 'works out the punishments', as if the road itself did it. 'Tartara' is a neuter plural form of 'Tartarus', the deepest pit of the underworld. The closing mark ends her speech.

sentences.t: Deiphobus contra: “Ne saevi, magna sacerdos;
sentences.l: Deiphobus in reply: “Do not be angry, great priestess;
sentences.i: Deiphobus answered: “Do not be harsh with me, great priestess;
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is left out again: 'Deiphobus contra (dixit)'. The opening mark begins his short last speech, 544–546. 'Ne saevi' is 'ne' with the imperative, a prohibition of verse and old Latin; prose would say 'noli saevire'. 'Deiphobus' is four syllables here, De-i-pho-bus, as in the last part.

sentences.t: discedam, explebo numerum, reddarque tenebris.
sentences.l: I will depart, I will fill out the number, and be given back to the darkness.
sentences.i: I am going; I will take my place again among the rest, and be returned to the darkness.
sentences.n: Three verbs, each a little further into the dark. 'Explebo numerum' is 'I will make up the number': most take it that he returns to the company of the shades and makes their count complete again; the phrase is short and has been read in other ways. 'Reddar' is the future passive, 'I shall be given back', and 'tenebris' is the dative.

sentences.t: I decus, i, nostrum; melioribus utere fatis!”
sentences.l: Go, glory, go, ours; better use fates!”
sentences.i: On your way, pride of our people, on your way; and may you have the use of kinder fates than mine!”
sentences.n: 'I' is the imperative of 'eo', 'go', said twice. 'Decus… nostrum' is split by the second 'i': 'our glory', 'pride of our people'. 'Utere' is the imperative of the deponent 'utor', which takes the ablative, 'melioribus… fatis', 'enjoy better fortunes', set against his own. The closing mark ends his speech.

sentences.t: Tantum effatus, et in verbo vestigia torsit.
sentences.l: So much having spoken, and on the word his steps he turned.
sentences.i: That was all he said, and with the word still on his lips he turned his steps away.
sentences.n: 'Tantum effatus (est)' is 'he said only so much'; 'effatus' is from the deponent 'effor'. 'In verbo' is 'on the word', with the last word still on his lips. 'Vestigia torsit' is 'turned his footsteps', a way of saying 'turned away'.

sentences.t:
Respicit Aeneas subito, et sub rupe sinistra
moenia lata videt, triplici circumdata muro,
quae rapidus flammis ambit torrentibus amnis,
Tartareus Phlegethon, torquetque sonantia saxa.
sentences.l:
Looks back Aeneas suddenly, and under a cliff on the left
walls broad he sees, with triple surrounded wall,
which swift with flames encircles rushing a river,
Tartarean Phlegethon, and whirls echoing rocks.
sentences.i: Suddenly Aeneas looked back, and saw beneath a cliff on the left a wide fortress girt with a triple wall, which a swift river of rushing flame flows round, Phlegethon of Tartarus, sending its rocks rolling and roaring.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Respicit… videt' are historic presents. 'Sinistra', 'on the left', is the side of the road to Tartarus (542). 'Moenia lata' is 'broad walls', a whole fortified city. 'Triplici… muro' frames 'circumdata', 'surrounded with a triple wall'. 'Quae… ambit' is 'which (the river) goes round'; 'rapidus… amnis' spans the line, with 'flammis… torrentibus' inside it, 'with torrents of flame'. Phlegethon, 'the blazing one' in Greek, is a river of fire in the underworld; Homer names it Pyriphlegethon, flowing into Acheron (Odyssey 10.513). 'Torquet' is 'whirls', 'rolls along', and 'sonantia saxa' is 'rocks that roar'.

sentences.i: In front stands a huge gate with pillars of solid adamant, which no strength of men and not even the dwellers in heaven themselves could tear out by war;
sentences.n: The verb is left out: 'porta adversa ingens (est)', 'there is a huge gate facing (them)'. 'Solido… adamante' is an ablative of material, 'columns of solid adamant': 'adamas', a Greek word, is the hardest of all substances, steel or diamond. 'Ut… valeant' is a clause of result, 'such that no force could'. 'Virum' is the old genitive plural of 'vir', 'of men' (you have seen it often). 'Non ipsi… caelicolae', 'not the heaven-dwellers themselves', is the gods, 'caelicola' being a compound of 'caelum' and 'colo'. 'Exscindere' is 'cut out', 'destroy utterly'.

sentences.t:
stat ferrea turris ad auras,
Tisiphoneque sedens, palla succincta cruenta,
vestibulum exsomnis servat noctesque diesque.
sentences.l:
stands an iron tower to the air,
and Tisiphone, sitting, with robe girt up bloody,
the entrance sleepless guards both nights and days.
sentences.i: an iron tower soars into the sky, and Tisiphone, seated there with her blood-stained robe girded up, keeps unsleeping watch over the entrance both night and day.
sentences.n: 'Stat… ad auras' is 'stands (rising) to the air'. Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, with Allecto and Megaera; her Greek name means 'avenger of murder'. 'Palla… cruenta' frames 'succincta', 'girt up in a bloody robe': the long robe is tucked up for action. 'Vestibulum' is the forecourt in front of the doors of a Roman house. 'Exsomnis' is 'sleepless'. 'Noctesque diesque' is the double '-que… -que', 'both nights and days', the accusative of duration of time.

sentences.t:
Hinc exaudiri gemitus, et saeva sonare
verbera; tum stridor ferri, tractaeque catenae.
sentences.l:
From here to be heard groans, and savage to sound
lashes; then the grating of iron, and dragged chains.
sentences.i: From within came the sound of groaning and the crack of savage lashes, then the screech of iron and the rattle of chains hauled along.
sentences.n: 'Exaudiri' and 'sonare' are historic infinitives, standing in for the imperfect indicative: 'groans were heard', 'lashes resounded'. Virgil uses them for a rush of sounds or actions. 'Saeva… verbera' runs over the line-end, 'savage blows (of the whip)'. 'Stridor ferri' is 'the shriek of iron', and 'tractae catenae', 'chains being dragged', with the verb left out.

sentences.t: Constitit Aeneas, strepitumque exterritus hausit.
sentences.l: Halted Aeneas, and the din, terrified, he drank in.
sentences.i: Aeneas stopped short, and stood terrified, drinking in the uproar.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Constitit' is the perfect of 'consisto', 'he stood still'. 'Exterritus' is 'thoroughly frightened'. 'Strepitum… hausit' is 'drank in the noise', 'haurio' used of taking something in through the senses.

sentences.t:
“Quae scelerum facies, O virgo, effare; quibusve
urguentur poenis?
sentences.l:
“What of the crimes are the forms, O maiden, speak out; or by what
are they pressed punishments?
sentences.i: “What kinds of wickedness are these, maiden? Tell me; and with what penalties are they hard pressed?
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Aeneas's question, 560–561. 'Quae scelerum facies' is 'what forms of crimes', with 'sint' understood in the indirect question. 'Virgo' is the Sibyl, a virgin priestess. 'Effare' is the imperative of 'effor', 'speak out'. '-ve' on 'quibusve' is 'or', and 'quibus' goes with 'poenis', held over the line-end. 'Urguentur' is Greenough's spelling of 'urgentur', 'are they pressed'.

sentences.t: Quis tantus plangor ad auras?”
sentences.l: What so great wailing to the air?”
sentences.i: What is that great lamenting that goes up to the sky?”
sentences.n: The verb is left out again: 'quis tantus plangor (it) ad auras', 'what wailing so loud (rises) to the air?' 'Plangor' is the beating of breasts and the wailing that goes with it. The closing mark ends Aeneas's question.

sentences.t:
Tum vates sic orsa loqui: “Dux inclute Teucrum,
nulli fas casto sceleratum insistere limen;
sentences.l:
Then the seer thus began to speak: “Leader renowned of the Teucrians,
for no one is it right, pure, upon the guilty to set foot threshold;
sentences.i: Then the prophetess began: “Famous leader of the Trojans, no one who is pure is permitted to step upon that criminal threshold;
sentences.n: 'Orsa (est)' is the perfect of the deponent 'ordior', 'began', with 'loqui', 'to speak'. The opening mark begins the Sibyl's long speech, which runs on into the next part. 'Inclute' is the vocative of 'inclutus', 'famous'. 'Teucrum' is the old genitive plural, 'of the Teucrians', the Trojans, with 'eu' a single Greek diphthong. 'Nulli… casto' is a dative with 'fas (est)', 'it is lawful for no pure person'. 'Insistere' takes the accusative here, 'to step upon'. 'Sceleratum… limen', 'the criminal threshold', frames the line-end: the place itself is called guilty.

sentences.t:
sed me cum lucis Hecate praefecit Avernis,
ipsa deum poenas docuit, perque omnia duxit.
sentences.l:
but me when of the groves Hecate set over the Avernian,
herself the gods' punishments taught, and through all led me.
sentences.i: but when Hecate set me in charge of the groves of Avernus, she herself taught me the punishments the gods inflict, and led me through them all.
sentences.n: 'Cum… praefecit' is 'when (Hecate) put (me) in charge of', with the dative 'lucis… Avernis', 'the groves of Avernus', the lake by Cumae near the entrance to the underworld. The Sibyl said the same at 118: Hecate, goddess of the crossroads and of the dead, gave her that office. 'Deum' is the genitive plural, 'the gods' punishments'. 'Docuit' takes two accusatives, 'me' and 'poenas', 'taught me the punishments'. The Sibyl has seen Tartarus; Aeneas, as a living and pious man, will only hear of it.

sentences.t:
Gnosius haec Rhadamanthus habet, durissima regna,
castigatque auditque dolos, subigitque fateri,
quae quis apud superos, furto laetatus inani,
distulit in seram commissa piacula mortem.
sentences.l:
Cnossian these Rhadamanthus holds, most harsh realms,
and he chastises and hears frauds, and forces them to confess
what anyone among those above, in theft rejoicing empty,
put off to late, committed, atonements, death.
sentences.i: Cretan Rhadamanthus rules this place, a kingdom without mercy; he punishes and hears out their deceits, and forces each to confess the sins he committed in the world above and, pleased with a secrecy that gained him nothing, left unatoned until death came too late.
sentences.n: 'Gnosius' is 'of Cnossos', the chief city of Crete (the Latin Library spells it 'Cnosius'). Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa and brother of Minos, was famous for justice; in Homer he lives in the Elysian plain (Odyssey 4.564), and Plato makes him one of the judges of the dead (Gorgias 524a). 'Haec… durissima regna' frames 'Rhadamanthus habet', 'holds these most pitiless realms'. 'Castigat… audit' puts punishment before the hearing, the natural order reversed (hysteron proteron), and the '-que… -que' pattern runs on to a third '-que' on 'subigit'. 'Subigit fateri' is 'forces (them) to confess'. 'Quae… piacula' is the object of 'fateri': 'piacula', strictly 'atonements', here the crimes that call for atonement, 'commissa', 'committed'. 'Quis' is the indefinite 'anyone' after the relative. 'Furto… inani' is 'with useless secrecy': he hid the crime and was glad, but it gained him nothing. 'Distulit in seram… mortem' is 'put off until a late death', too late for atonement.

sentences.t:
Continuo sontes ultrix accincta flagello
Tisiphone quatit insultans, torvosque sinistra
intentans angues vocat agmina saeva sororum.
sentences.l:
At once the guilty the avenger, girt with a whip,
Tisiphone strikes, leaping on them, and grim in her left hand
brandishing snakes, calls the troops savage of her sisters.
sentences.i: At once Tisiphone the avenger, armed with her lash, falls on the guilty and scourges them with scorn, and holding out her grim snakes in her left hand she calls up the savage band of her sisters.
sentences.n: 'Continuo' is 'immediately', the sentence following at once on the confession. 'Sontes', 'the guilty', is the '-es' accusative plural ('sontis' in the Latin Library). 'Ultrix', 'the avenger', is in apposition to Tisiphone, who guards the gate (555). 'Accincta flagello' is 'girded with a whip'. 'Quatit' is 'shakes', 'lashes', and 'insultans' is 'leaping upon them', 'trampling', 'mocking'. 'Torvos… angues' frames 'sinistra intentans', 'stretching out grim snakes in her left hand': the Furies wear and carry serpents. 'Angues' is 'anguis' in the Latin Library. 'Agmina saeva sororum' is 'the savage columns of her sisters', the other Furies.

sentences.t:
Tum demum horrisono stridentes cardine sacrae
panduntur portae.
sentences.l:
Then at last, with horrid-sounding grating on the hinge, the accursed
are thrown open gates.
sentences.i: Then, and not till then, the accursed gates swing wide, their hinges shrieking with a hideous noise.
sentences.n: 'Tum demum' is 'then and only then'. 'Horrisono… cardine' is 'on hinge of horrid sound', 'horrisonus' a compound adjective of the old epic kind. 'Stridentes' is 'shrieking', 'grinding'. 'Sacrae' is 'accursed': 'sacer' is 'set apart for a god', and so, of the gods below, 'doomed', 'cursed'. The subject 'portae' is held back until the next line.

sentences.t:
Cernis custodia qualis
vestibulo sedeat, facies quae limina servet?
sentences.l:
Do you see guard of what kind
in the entrance sits, what shape the threshold guards?
sentences.i: Do you see what sort of sentry sits in the forecourt, what a form keeps watch upon the threshold?
sentences.n: 'Cernis' introduces two indirect questions with the subjunctive, 'qualis… sedeat' and 'quae… servet'. 'Custodia' is 'guard', the abstract for the person, Tisiphone (555–556). 'Vestibulo' is an ablative of place. 'Facies' is 'shape', 'figure', and 'quae' agrees with it.

sentences.t:
Quinquaginta atris immanis hiatibus Hydra
saevior intus habet sedem.
sentences.l:
Fifty with black, monstrous, gapings the Hydra,
more savage, within has its seat.
sentences.i: Within lives the Hydra, crueller still, monstrous with fifty black yawning throats.
sentences.n: 'Quinquaginta atris… hiatibus' is an ablative of description, 'with fifty black gaping mouths', framing 'immanis'. The Hydra was the many-headed water-snake of Lerna, killed by Hercules; one 'belua Lernae' already stands among the monsters at the entrance (287). 'Saevior', 'fiercer' (than Tisiphone), 'intus', 'inside': this is a second and worse one, within the gates.

sentences.t:
Tum Tartarus ipse
bis patet in praeceps tantum tenditque sub umbras,
quantus ad aetherium caeli suspectus Olympum.
sentences.l:
Then Tartarus itself
twice lies open sheer down as far and stretches beneath the shades
as great as to the heavenly of the sky the upward view Olympus.
sentences.i: Beyond, Tartarus itself drops away sheer and runs down under the shadows twice as far as the eye looks up through the sky to Olympus in the heavens.
sentences.n: 'Tum' is 'next', in space. 'Bis… tantum… quantus' is the correlative 'twice as far… as'. 'Patet in praeceps' is 'opens headlong', 'drops sheer down'. 'Suspectus' is a noun here, 'the upward look', 'the view upwards', with 'est' understood. 'Ad aetherium… Olympum' frames 'caeli suspectus', 'to airy Olympus', the gods' home in the sky. Hesiod puts Tartarus as far beneath the earth as heaven is above it (Theogony 720), and in the Iliad (8.13–16) Zeus threatens to hurl a god into Tartarus, as far below Hades as heaven is above earth; Virgil's 'twice' doubles Hesiod's measure and comes to much the same as Homer's.

sentences.t:
Hic genus antiquum Terrae, Titania pubes,
fulmine deiecti fundo volvuntur in imo.
sentences.l:
Here the race ancient of Earth, the Titan youth,
by the thunderbolt hurled down, in the depth roll lowest.
sentences.i: Here the ancient brood of Earth, the young Titans, flung down by the thunderbolt, writhe at the very bottom.
sentences.n: 'Hic' is 'here'. 'Genus antiquum Terrae' is 'the ancient offspring of Earth', the Titans, children of Earth and Heaven, who fought the Olympian gods and were cast down by Jupiter into Tartarus, as Hesiod tells in the Theogony. 'Titania pubes' is in apposition, 'the Titan youth', 'pubes' being the young men of a people. 'Fulmine' is an ablative of means. 'Fundo… in imo' is 'at the lowest bottom'. 'Volvuntur' is 'roll', 'writhe'.

sentences.t:
Hic et Aloidas geminos immania vidi
corpora, qui manibus magnum rescindere caelum
adgressi, superisque Iovem detrudere regnis.
sentences.l:
Here also the Aloidae twin, huge I saw
bodies, who with their hands the great to tear down heaven
attempted, and from the upper Jove to thrust realms.
sentences.i: Here too I saw the twin sons of Aloeus, monstrous in size, who set their hands to tearing down the great sky and thrusting Jupiter out of his kingdom above.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, though the Sibyl is still speaking. 'Aloidas' is a Greek accusative plural, 'the sons of Aloeus': Otus and Ephialtes, giants who piled Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to climb to heaven. Homer tells of them in Odyssey 11.305–320, where Apollo kills them before they are grown. 'Immania… corpora' is in apposition, 'huge bodies'. 'Vidi', 'I saw', is the Sibyl's own: Hecate led her through Tartarus (565). 'Adgressi (sunt)' is 'set about', 'attempted', Greenough's spelling of 'aggressi'. 'Rescindere' is 'to tear open', 'pull down'. 'Superis… regnis' is an ablative of separation, 'from the realms above'.

sentences.t:
Vidi et crudeles dantem Salmonea poenas,
dum flammas Iovis et sonitus imitatur Olympi.
sentences.l:
I saw also, cruel paying Salmoneus penalties,
while the flames of Jove and the sounds he imitates of Olympus.
sentences.i: I saw Salmoneus too, paying a cruel penalty for mimicking the fire of Jupiter and the thunders of Olympus.
sentences.n: 'Dare poenas' is 'to pay a penalty', 'to be punished'. 'Salmonea' is a Greek accusative. Salmoneus was a son of Aeolus who ruled in Elis; he is the father of Tyro in Odyssey 11.236, but his crime comes from later stories. 'Crudeles' is 'crudelis' in the Latin Library. 'Dum… imitatur' is 'dum' with the present, the regular tense with 'dum', 'while', even of past time: 'while he was imitating'. He was struck down in the very act (592–594), and pays for it here. 'Flammas Iovis' is the lightning, 'sonitus Olympi' the thunder.

sentences.t:
Quattuor hic invectus equis et lampada quassans
per Graium populos mediaeque per Elidis urbem
ibat ovans, divomque sibi poscebat honorem,—
sentences.l:
Drawn by four this man horses, and a torch brandishing,
through the Greeks' peoples and through mid Elis' city
was going in triumph, and the gods' for himself demanded honour,—
sentences.i: He drove in a four-horse chariot, brandishing a torch, through the peoples of Greece and through the city at the heart of Elis, riding in triumph and claiming for himself the honours of the gods,
sentences.n: 'Hic' is the pronoun, 'he', with 'invectus', 'carried in (a chariot)'. 'Quattuor… equis' is an ablative of means framing it. 'Lampada' is a Greek accusative of 'lampas', 'torch'. 'Graium' is the old genitive plural of 'Graius', 'of the Greeks'. 'Mediae… Elidis urbem' is 'the city in the middle of Elis', the region of the Peloponnese where Olympia lies. 'Ovans' is 'in triumph', the word for a lesser Roman triumph. 'Divom' is the genitive plural again, 'the honour of the gods', 'divine honours'. Greenough's dash breaks off the description for the outburst that follows.

sentences.t:
demens, qui nimbos et non imitabile fulmen
aere et cornipedum pulsu simularet equorum.
sentences.l:
madman, who storm-clouds and the not imitable thunderbolt
with bronze and the beat of horn-footed would counterfeit horses.
sentences.i: madman, to think he could counterfeit the storm-clouds and the lightning no one can copy with clashing bronze and the hoofbeats of his horses.
sentences.n: 'Demens' is in apposition to the subject, 'madman!', the Sibyl's own comment. 'Qui… simularet' is a relative clause of cause, 'since he tried to counterfeit'; the subjunctive gives the reason for 'demens'. 'Non imitabile' is 'inimitable'. 'Aere' is 'with bronze': the stories made him drive over a bronze bridge or drag bronze to sound like thunder. 'Cornipedum… equorum' frames 'pulsu simularet', 'the beat of horn-footed horses', 'cornipes' a compound adjective for horses' hoofs.

sentences.t:
At pater omnipotens densa inter nubila telum
contorsit, non ille faces nec fumea taedis
lumina, praecipitemque immani turbine adegit.
sentences.l:
But the father almighty amid dense clouds a bolt
hurled, not he torches nor smoky with pine-brands
lights, and headlong with a vast whirlwind drove him.
sentences.i: But the almighty father hurled his own bolt from the thick clouds, no torch, no smoky flare of pine, and sent him spinning headlong in a vast blast of fire.
sentences.n: 'At' sets the true thunderer against the false. 'Pater omnipotens' is Jupiter. 'Densa inter nubila' has 'inter' set between adjective and noun, 'amid the thick clouds'. 'Contorsit' is 'whirled', 'hurled'. 'Non ille faces…' is a scornful aside: 'not he (hurled) torches', as Salmoneus did; 'ille' is Jupiter. 'Fumea taedis / lumina' is 'lights smoky with pine-wood', run over the line-end. 'Praecipitem' is 'headlong', agreeing with the unexpressed 'eum', Salmoneus. 'Immani turbine' is 'with a huge whirlwind', the blast of the bolt. 'Adegit' is 'drove (him) down'.

sentences.t:
Nec non et Tityon, Terrae omniparentis alumnum,
cernere erat, per tota novem cui iugera corpus
porrigitur,
sentences.l:
And not not also Tityos, of Earth the all-mothering nursling,
to see it was, over whole nine whose acres the body
is stretched,
sentences.i: Tityos, too, child of Earth the mother of all, could be seen there, his body covering nine whole acres as it lies,
sentences.n: 'Nec non et' is 'and also', the two negatives cancelling each other. 'Tityon' is a Greek accusative. 'Terrae omniparentis alumnum' is 'nursling of all-producing Earth': the giant Tityos was born of, or reared by, Earth. 'Cernere erat' is 'it was possible to see', 'erat' standing for 'licebat', a Greek turn of phrase. 'Cui… corpus porrigitur' is 'whose body is stretched out', 'cui' a dative of reference. 'Per tota novem… iugera' is 'over nine whole iugera', a Roman land measure of about two-thirds of an acre. The model is Odyssey 11.576–581, where Odysseus sees Tityos lying over nine 'plethra', two vultures tearing his liver for his violence against Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis. The sentence is long and is split here at a comma.

sentences.t:
rostroque immanis voltur obunco
immortale iecur tondens fecundaque poenis
viscera, rimaturque epulis, habitatque sub alto
pectore, nec fibris requies datur ulla renatis.
sentences.l:
and with beak a monstrous vulture hooked
his deathless liver cropping, and fertile for punishments
his entrails, both searches for its banquets, and dwells under the deep
breast, nor to the fibres rest is given any reborn.
sentences.i: and a monstrous vulture with hooked beak, cropping his undying liver and his vitals that breed new torment, probes them for its meals and lives deep in his breast, and the fibres, as they grow again, are given no rest.
sentences.n: 'Rostro… obunco', 'with hooked beak', frames 'immanis voltur'; 'voltur' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultur'. Virgil has one vulture where Homer has two. 'Tondens' is 'cropping', 'shearing', as a beast crops grass. 'Immortale iecur' is 'the undying liver', which always grows back; the liver was thought the seat of desire. 'Fecunda poenis' is 'fruitful for punishment', 'poenis' a dative: the more it grows, the more there is to suffer. 'Rimatur epulis' is 'searches (them) for feasts', 'epulis' a dative of purpose. 'Habitat' is 'makes its home', the bird never leaves. 'Fibris… renatis' is a dative, 'to the reborn fibres', the regrown flesh of the liver.

sentences.t: [Quid memorem Lapithas, Ixiona Pirithoumque?]
sentences.l: [Why should I mention the Lapiths, Ixion and Pirithous?]
sentences.i: [Why should I speak of the Lapiths, of Ixion and Pirithous?]
sentences.n: Greenough brackets this line as spurious, so it stands here inside [ ]. 'Quid memorem' is a deliberative subjunctive, 'why should I tell of', a formula for passing over (praeteritio). 'Ixiona' is a Greek accusative; 'Pirithoum' is the ordinary Latin one. The Lapiths were a people of Thessaly, ruled by Ixion and then by his son Pirithous; they fought the Centaurs at Pirithous's wedding. Ixion was bound on a turning wheel for his insolence towards Juno, and Pirithous went down with Theseus to carry off Proserpina (397). The trouble is that the punishment described next, a rock overhanging a feast, is in other accounts the punishment of Tantalus, and without this line 'quos' would have no antecedent; editors have suspected a gap here.

sentences.t:
quos super atra silex iam iam lapsura cadentique
imminet adsimilis;
sentences.l:
over whom a black flint, any moment now about to slip, and to one falling
hangs, like;
sentences.i: Above them a dark rock hangs, forever on the point of sliding down, and looks as if it were already falling;
sentences.n: 'Quos super' is 'over whom', the preposition placed after its pronoun; Greenough prints 'quos' with a small letter, so that it reads straight on from the question. 'Silex', 'flint', 'rock', is feminine here, with 'atra' and 'lapsura'. 'Iam iam' is 'now, now', 'at any moment'. 'Cadenti… adsimilis' is 'like one falling', 'adsimilis' with the dative. 'Cadentique' ends the line with a '-que' that is one syllable too many: it is elided into 'imminet', the first word of the next line, a rare licence called a hypermetric line. 'Imminet' is 'hangs over', 'threatens'.

sentences.i: the golden frames of high banqueting couches gleam, and a feast laid out with a king's splendour stands before their eyes;
sentences.n: 'Lucent' is placed first, 'there gleam'. 'Genialibus altis… toris' runs over the line-end, 'on high festal couches': 'genialis' is 'belonging to the Genius', and so of feasting and of marriage. 'Aurea fulcra' are the gilded frames or legs of the dining-couches. 'Epulae… paratae' is 'banquets prepared'. 'Ante ora' is 'before their faces'. 'Regifico luxu' is an ablative of manner, 'with royal luxury'. The scene recalls Homer's Tantalus, who stands in a pool, with fruit and water always snatched from him (Odyssey 11.582–592); the stone hung over Tantalus is in Pindar (Olympian 1).

sentences.t:
Furiarum maxima iuxta
accubat, et manibus prohibet contingere mensas,
exsurgitque facem attollens, atque intonat ore.
sentences.l:
the of the Furies greatest close by
reclines, and with their hands forbids to touch the tables,
and rises up, a torch lifting, and thunders with her mouth.
sentences.i: the eldest of the Furies lies at table close beside them, and keeps them from laying a hand on the board, and springs up, raising her torch high, and thunders at them.
sentences.n: 'Furiarum maxima' is 'the greatest (or eldest) of the Furies', not named. 'Iuxta' is an adverb, 'close by'. 'Accubat' is 'reclines at table', the Roman posture for dining, so she sits among them as one of the guests. 'Prohibet contingere' is 'forbids (them) to touch', and 'manibus' is 'with their hands'. 'Exsurgit… attollens' is 'rises, lifting her torch'. 'Intonat ore' is 'thunders with her mouth', a terrible shout. The Sibyl's account continues in the next part.
